lessons.title: Multiply and divide algebraic powers
lessons.summary: Group powers by their letter base, calculate the coefficient separately and simplify algebraic quotients.
lessons.objective: Group powers by their letter base, calculate the coefficient separately and simplify algebraic quotients.
lessons.before: Recall what a power means from Indices I. The same factor-counting rules work for a letter base.
lessons.ideas:
Use \(x^m x^n=x^{m+n}\). A letter on its own contributes one factor, so \(x=x^1\). Multiply the ordinary numerical coefficients separately.

For \(x\ne0\), use \(\frac{x^m}{x^n}=x^{m-n}\). Subtract the denominator index from the numerator index. Divide the coefficients as a separate calculation.

In \(5x^3y\cdot 2xy^4\), group the two coefficient factors, the copies of \(x\) and the copies of \(y\). The result is \(10x^4y^5\).
lessons.method:
How do I join powers of the same letter?

A power counts repeated factors. In a product of powers of the same letter, all the copies of that letter belong to one group.

What does the denominator remove?

A common nonzero factor can be cancelled from the top and bottom of a fraction. Cross off one pair at a time if a quotient is new to you.

How do I handle more than one letter?

In an expression built from products or quotients, sort the factors into their numerical parts and one group per letter.
mistakes: Adding two terms is different from multiplying their factors. For example, \(x^2+x^2=2x^2\). The expression \(x^2x^2\) is \(x^4\).
The order of subtraction follows the fraction. Reversing top and bottom changes the resulting power.
Do not add the indices of different bases. The powers of \(x\) provide no extra factors of \(y\).

examples.title: Join matching groups of factors
examples.question: Write \(x^{2}\times x^{3}\) in the form \(x^{p}\). Give \(p\).
examples.solution:
The base is \(x\) in both factors. Count all the copies of this base.

Add the indices using \(2+3=5\).

The result is \(x^{5}\), so \(p=5\).

examples.title: Cancel the matching factors in a quotient
examples.question: For \(x\ne0\), Write \(\frac{x^{9}}{x^{2}}\) in the form \(x^{p}\). Give \(p\).
examples.solution:
Because \(x\ne 0\), cancel one matching factor at a time.

The number of factors remaining above the bar is \(9-2=7\).

The result is \(x^{7}\), so \(p=7\).

examples.title: Group two different letter bases
examples.question: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(2x^{3}y^{2}\times 3x^{2}y\) as \(cx^{p}y^{q}\). Give \(c\), \(p\) and \(q\).
examples.solution:
Group the counts for \(x\) and \(y\) separately. The lone \(y\) contributes one factor.

The numerical product is \(6\). The indices are \(3+2\) and \(2+1\).

The simplified expression is \(6x^{5}y^{3}\). In the requested form, \(c=6\), \(p=5\), \(q=3\).

lessons.title: Powers of products, zero and negative indices
lessons.summary: Apply an outer power to an entire bracket and use reciprocals to write positive indices.
lessons.objective: Apply an outer power to an entire bracket and use reciprocals to write positive indices.
lessons.before: Separate numerical coefficients from letter bases. Recall zero and negative numerical powers from Indices I.
lessons.ideas:
Use \((cx^m)^n=c^n x^{mn}\). The outer power acts on the coefficient as well as the letter. If the bracket contains a quotient, simplify the quotient first when possible.

For a nonzero base \(A\), \(A^0=1\). If a bracket has exponent zero, first identify the whole bracket as the base.

Compare \(4x^{-3}=\frac{4}{x^3}\) and \((4x^3)^{-1}=\frac{1}{4x^3}\). For a quotient, subtract the indices first and then convert any remaining negative power to a reciprocal.
lessons.method:
What exactly does an outside index act on?

A whole bracket raised to a power behaves as one base. Read the brackets before deciding what the outside index applies to.

Why does a zero exponent give one?

Dividing a nonzero power by itself gives one. The quotient law also gives the difference of two identical indices, which is zero.

Which factor moves when the exponent is negative?

A negative exponent makes a reciprocal of the matching positive power. The scope may be one letter or a whole bracket.
mistakes: In \((4x^2)^3\), the multiplier becomes \(4^3\). It is easy to cube only the letter and accidentally retain 4.
A zero exponent does not make the expression zero. If the base is zero, the rule does not apply.
Moving a negative-index factor through the fraction bar changes its exponent sign. It does not change the sign of the factor's coefficient.

examples.title: Raise every factor inside the brackets
examples.question: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(\left(2x^{3}\right)^{2}\) as \(cx^{p}\). Give \(c\) and \(p\).
examples.solution:
Repeat the entire product inside the brackets \(2\) times.

The numerical factor becomes \(2^{2}=4\). The two powers on the letter combine to \(3\times 2=6\).

The simplified expression is \(4x^{6}\). In the requested form, \(c=4\), \(p=6\).

examples.title: Simplify a quotient before raising it
examples.question: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(\left(\frac{2x^{3}}{2x}\right)^{3}\) as \(cx^{p}\). Give \(c\) and \(p\).
examples.solution:
Inside the bracket the coefficients cancel. The quotient of letters becomes \(x^{2}\).

Then apply the outside power. The indices multiply to \(2\times 3=6\).

The simplified expression is \(x^{6}\). In the requested form, \(c=1\), \(p=6\).

examples.title: Take the reciprocal of a powered bracket
examples.question: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(\left(2x^{2}\right)^{-2}\) as \(\frac{c}{x^{p}}\). Give \(c\) and \(p\). Use positive indices in the final expression.
examples.solution:
First write the reciprocal of the square of the whole bracket.

The square in the denominator is \(4x^{4}\). The coefficient in the requested template is \(\frac{1}{4}\).

The simplified expression is \(\frac{1}{4x^{4}}\). In the requested form, \(c=\frac{1}{4}\), \(p=4\).

lessons.title: Find an unknown index
lessons.summary: Write both sides as powers of the same base and solve a direct equation for an index.
lessons.objective: Write both sides as powers of the same base and solve a direct equation for an index.
lessons.before: Recall familiar powers such as \(3^4=81\) and the meaning of a zero or negative index.
lessons.ideas:
With base greater than 1, the powers increase as their indices increase. Two equal powers of that fixed base have equal indices. For example, \(2^x=128\) becomes \(2^x=2^7\).

Rewrite \(\frac{1}{a^n}\) as \(a^{-n}\). If you see \(a^x=1\), the matching power is \(a^0\), provided \(a>1\).

Add indices in a product and subtract them in a quotient. After matching bases, solve the equation between the resulting index expressions.
lessons.method:
How do I find a shared base?

Read the known base beside the unknown index. The other side must be expressed as a power of that same base before the indices can be compared.

What if the right-hand side is one or a fraction?

A power of a base greater than 1 is one when its index is zero. A positive answer smaller than one comes from a negative index.

What if a side contains a product or quotient?

A product or quotient of powers of the same base can be written as a single power. Then it is possible to match the index with the single power on the other side.
mistakes: Dividing the right-hand number by the base once does not find its index. Look for repeated multiplication by the base.
A fraction on the right does not force the unknown index to be a fractional number. An integer such as \(-2\) can give an exact reciprocal.
A quotient subtracts the index in its denominator. An index attached to a power is not a numerical multiplier outside it.

examples.title: Match a base to an integer power
examples.question: Solve \(2^{x}=8\).
examples.solution:
Build powers of \(2\) by multiplying by one more copy of the base each time.

Write the right-hand side as \(2^{3}\). Match the two index values.

The solution is \(x=3\).

examples.title: Match an exact reciprocal power
examples.question: Solve \(2^{x}=\frac{1}{2}\).
examples.solution:
The denominator is \(2^{1}\).

An exact reciprocal of a positive power is \(2^{-1}\). Match its index to \(x\).

The solution is \(x=-1\).

examples.title: Restore a subtracted index
examples.question: Solve \(\frac{3^{x}}{3^{2}}=3^{4}\).
examples.solution:
Subtract the denominator index in the quotient, giving \(3^{x-2}\).

Equate the indices and add \(2\) to both sides of \(x-2=4\).

The solution is \(x=6\).

lessons.title: Algebraic fractional indices (Extended)
lessons.summary: Take roots of positive algebraic factors and add, subtract or multiply fractional exponents exactly.
lessons.objective: Take roots of positive algebraic factors and add, subtract or multiply fractional exponents exactly.
lessons.before: Extend the numerical root and power rules from Indices I. Here the letter bases in fractional powers are positive.
lessons.ideas:
For \(x>0\), \(x^{\frac{m}{n}}=(\sqrt[n]{x})^m\). If the base is a positive product, the root and the power act on all its factors.

Use a common denominator for addition and subtraction. For example, \(\frac{x^{\frac34}}{x^{-\frac12}}=x^{\frac54}\) since \(\frac34-(-\frac12)=\frac54\).

When the power acts on a product, use the positive root and power on each factor. Take the reciprocal of the complete result.
lessons.method:
Which part of a fractional index tells me the root?

Read the denominator of the index as the order of the root. Read the numerator as the power. With positive bases, taking the root first often makes the arithmetic shorter.

How do I combine fractional indices with the same base?

The index laws for multiplication and division still apply to positive bases when the indices are fractions. Each arithmetic operation is performed on the indices.

How do I use a negative fractional index?

First find the corresponding positive fractional power. A negative fractional power is its reciprocal, provided the base is positive.
mistakes: The square root of an arbitrary square is its non-negative magnitude. For a letter known to be positive, \(\sqrt{x^2}=x\).
Subtract the entire denominator exponent, including its sign. A number outside a power is a coefficient and is treated separately.
The minus sign on an index changes which side of a fraction holds the factor. It does not make the base or the result negative.

examples.title: Take a root of an algebraic power
examples.question: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(\left(4x^{4}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}\) as \(cx^{p}\). Give \(c\) and \(p\).
examples.solution:
The root of order \(2\) gives \(2x^{2}\). This uses the positive value of \(x\).

Raise both of those factors to \(3\), giving coefficient \(8\) and index \(6\).

The simplified expression is \(8x^{6}\). In the requested form, \(c=8\), \(p=6\).

examples.title: Add fractional indices with the same base
examples.question: Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(2x^{\frac{1}{2}}\times 3x^{\frac{3}{2}}\) as \(cx^{p}\). Give \(c\) and \(p\).
examples.solution:
Multiply the numerical coefficients to get \(6\).

Use a common denominator to add the two indices: \(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{3}{2}=2\).

The simplified expression is \(6x^{2}\). In the requested form, \(c=6\), \(p=2\).

examples.title: Use a reciprocal after taking the root
examples.question: For \(x>0\), write \(\left(4x^{4}\right)^{-\frac{3}{2}}\) as \(\frac{1}{cx^{p}}\) with \(c>0\) and \(p>0\). Give \(c\) and \(p\).
examples.solution:
The positive exponent of the same size gives \(8x^{6}\). Take the root of order \(2\) before raising to \(3\).

The original index is negative. Take the reciprocal of the whole result to obtain \(\frac{1}{8x^{6}}\).

lessons.title: Solve equal-base exponential equations (Extended)
lessons.summary: Rewrite different bases using one common base, then solve the linear equation in the two indices.
lessons.objective: Rewrite different bases using one common base, then solve the linear equation in the two indices.
lessons.before: Use the laws for a power of a power and for negative exponents. Be comfortable solving a linear equation in one unknown.
lessons.ideas:
When rewriting \((a^m)^{kx+d}\), multiply the whole index by \(m\). Write \(a^{m(kx+d)}\) before expanding or matching the indices.

With \(a>1\), \(\left(\frac1a\right)^{x+d}=a^{-(x+d)}\). If there are several terms in the exponent, the minus sign applies to the entire group.

Move the unknown terms to one side and the constants to the other. Be prepared for a zero, negative or fractional answer.
lessons.method:
How do I rewrite a larger base?

If one base is a positive integer power of the other, use the smaller base. Sometimes both displayed bases are powers of a still smaller number.

What if one base is a reciprocal?

A reciprocal of the chosen base is its exponent minus one. Raising that reciprocal to an unknown power multiplies the new exponent by minus one.

What if both sides still have an unknown?

After expressing all factors with the same base, combine each side into a single power. Only then compare the indices.
mistakes: Each term of an index bracket is multiplied. Rewriting the base can change both the coefficient of \(x\) and the constant term.
A reciprocal base is not a negative base. Its value stays positive, but its rewritten index changes sign.
Do not equate indices while the displayed bases are different. Check that both sides have the same base after any products or quotients are simplified.

examples.title: Compare an unknown index with a fractional power
examples.question: Solve \(4^{x}=2^{1}\).
examples.solution:
Rewrite the base on the left as \(2^{2}\), so the left-hand index over base \(2\) is \(2x\).

The indices must match. Solve \(2x=1\).

The solution is \(x=\frac{1}{2}\).

examples.title: Use a reciprocal base before matching indices
examples.question: Solve \(\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^{x}=3^{2x+2}\).
examples.solution:
The reciprocal base is \(3^{-1}\). Raising it to \(x\) gives \(3^{-x}\).

Set \(-x=2x+2\). Rearrange to \(3x=-2\).

The solution is \(x=-\frac{2}{3}\).

examples.title: Handle a quotient and a negative coefficient of x
examples.question: Solve \(\frac{4^{x}}{2^{1}}=2^{-x+2}\).
examples.solution:
Rewrite the numerator as \(2^{2x}\). Subtract the denominator index \(1\).

The resulting index equation is \(2x-1=-x+2\). Collect the two terms that contain \(x\).

The solution is \(x=1\).

questions.title: Combine a product and a quotient

questions.solution_html:
In the numerator the index of \(x\) is \(7+1\) and the index of \(y\) is \(1+5\).

Now subtract the denominator's indices \(2\) and \(1\). The common coefficient \(2\) cancels.

The simplified expression is \(6x^{6}y^{5}\). In the requested form, \(c=6\), \(p=6\), \(q=5\).

Now subtract the denominator's indices \(2\) and \(1\). The common coefficient \(3\) cancels.

The simplified expression is \(7x^{7}y^{2}\). In the requested form, \(c=7\), \(p=7\), \(q=2\).

questions.title: Join powers and use the unwritten index
questions.prompt_html:
1. Write \(x^{9}\times x^{6}\) in the form \(x^{p}\). Give \(p\).

    Write the complete simplified expression as well as the requested values. Show your working.

    [2]

  2. Assume all letters used as bases are positive. Write \(11x\times 4x^{10}\) as \(cx^{p}\). Give \(c\) and \(p\).

    Write the complete simplified expression as well as the requested values. Show your working.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The base is \(x\) in both factors. Count all the copies of this base.

Add the indices using \(9+6=15\).

The result is \(x^{15}\), so \(p=15\).

(b)

The first \(x\) contributes one factor. The second term contributes \(10\) factors of \(x\).

Multiply the number parts to get \(44\). Add the two index values separately.

The simplified expression is \(44x^{11}\). In the requested form, \(c=44\), \(p=11\).
questions.hint_html:
(a) Add the counts of matching factors when the powers are multiplied.

(b) A letter written without a visible index has index one.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the product law for two powers with the same base.
Give the complete exact result. \(x^{15}\) Any algebraically valid method earns the same credit.
Multiply the numerical factors and include the single factor from the first term.
Give the complete exact result. \(44x^{11}\) Any algebraically valid method earns the same credit.
